title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Water
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Water utilities in at least twelve states have now reported PLC attacks, with pressure loss and boil-water notices
items.content_text: Federal and state authorities are still working through a coordinated campaign against internet-facing programmable logic controllers at drinking water and wastewater utilities. It surfaced when more than 30 Minnesota community water systems were hit over the weekend of 26 and 27 July; the FBI and EPA then reported incidents in at least seven states, and utilities in at least twelve have since been affected, including Michigan, Georgia, South Dakota and New Jersey. After reaching devices remotely the actors change IP addresses and set passwords, stripping operators of monitoring and control. Reported operational effects include loss of pressure, flooding, boil-water advisories and sustained manual operation. Federal agencies have not formally attributed the activity; multiple sources point to Iran-nexus groups, and a group calling itself APT Iran has claimed the Minnesota attacks.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: FBI/EPA public service announcement and CISA alerts — corroborated by Cybersecurity Dive, The Record and SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: PSA issued 30 Jul 2026, updated 6 Aug 2026; latest reporting 20 Aug 2026

items.title: Five agencies warn AI-written scripts are reading Siemens S7 controllers, with water named a top target sector
items.content_text: The NSA, CISA, FBI, Department of Energy and EPA issued a joint advisory on 19 August warning that threat actors are pairing the open-source snap7 and python-snap7 automation libraries with AI-assisted scripting to build custom tools that mimic legitimate OT monitoring software. Those tools provide read and write access to Siemens S7 controller memory, configuration data and ladder logic over the S7comm protocol. Water and wastewater is named among the most-targeted sectors alongside critical manufacturing, energy, chemical, food and agriculture, and commercial facilities. The agencies state plainly that this is an active threat rather than a theoretical one, and that using AI to generate exploitation scripts sharply reduces the expertise and time an actor needs. Affected lines run from the legacy S7-200 and S7-300 through the S7-1200 and S7-1500, including F-series safety controllers. The agencies assess the current activity as reconnaissance and capability development, with read access being used to understand target environments and prepare for later write operations.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Joint advisory AA26-231A (NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE, EPA) — corroborated by SecurityWeek and Help Net Security

items.title: What the attacks actually did: lost view, altered ladder logic, pressure loss and flooding
items.content_text: The FBI and EPA public service announcement, issued 30 July and last updated 6 August, describes the observed technique in enough detail to be useful operationally. Actors targeted internet-exposed Rockwell Automation and Allen-Bradley MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 controllers, remotely tampering with device configuration by changing IP addresses and enabling and setting passwords. The result was loss of view, and in some cases loss of function, over connected equipment. At least one organisation reported modified PLC project files after noticing ladder-logic discrepancies across several of its sites. The agencies also note that similarities in network setups provided by third parties may let an actor repeat a success across multiple customers of the same integrator. Reported operational effects included loss of pressure and flooding, with the agencies pointing out that pressure loss can allow untreated ground water to seep into distribution pipes. How badly a utility was affected depended on whether the device monitored or controlled equipment, and on whether staff could switch to manual.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: FBI and EPA public service announcement

items.title: Attribution remains unofficial: claimed by APT Iran, suspected Iran-nexus, not formally confirmed
items.content_text: Federal agencies have deliberately not attributed the water campaign publicly. Multiple sources, and most reporting, point to Iran-nexus groups, on the basis that Iranian-affiliated actors have repeatedly targeted the specific kinds of operational technology used in water and wastewater since 2023 — including the CyberAv3ngers campaign against Unitronics controllers. Minnesota officials described the July attacks as coordinated but said it was not clear whether all of them were carried out by the same actor. Earlier this month a group calling itself APT Iran claimed credit for the Minnesota attacks and said it was working with CyberAv3ngers, according to Check Point Research; the same claim asserted access to power grids and telecommunications systems, which has not been substantiated. Separately, the Justice Department unsealed charges on 18 August against 17 people over an IRGC-linked intellectual property theft campaign — different activity, but part of the same attribution backdrop. Treat all of this as claimed or assessed, not proven.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Cybersecurity Dive, citing Check Point Research and Minnesota IT Services

items.title: Industrial ransomware up 12 percent in Q2, and it does not need the control system to disrupt operations
items.content_text: Dragos recorded 1,140 ransomware incidents at industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up from 1,020 in the first quarter. Manufacturing took 747 of them, with construction at 176, equipment manufacturing at 114 and food and beverage at 70. The finding that transfers most directly to water utilities is not the count but the mechanism: disrupting the IT systems that support an industrial environment is frequently enough to interrupt operations even when the attackers never reach the control system. Extortion also kept shifting away from file encryption toward data theft. For a utility that means billing, customer service, laboratory information management, work order and compliance reporting systems — the ones that would stop you issuing a boil-water notice efficiently, or producing regulatory sampling records, while treatment itself keeps running normally.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Dragos Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis — via Help Net Security

items.title: Rockwell advisory on MicroLogix tampering includes a recovery procedure that erases the program
items.content_text: Rockwell Automation issued an advisory warning customers about actors targeting its MicroLogix 1400 series devices, published alongside the federal alerts. The company confirmed that attackers have been able to change IP addresses and modify passwords, blocking water system operators from monitoring their own devices. Its recovery guidance for a tampered device is blunt: cycle power, then remove and reinstall the battery. That procedure clears the IP address and the program, which is exactly why the advisory pairs it with a recommendation to create offline backups and remove the devices from the public internet. The practical point for a utility with a small distribution estate is that recovery is not a software reset — it means a truck roll to each affected panel and a verified program download, so the value of having current, verified offline copies of every project file is immediate rather than theoretical.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Rockwell Automation PSIRT advisory SD1790 — reported by Cybersecurity Dive
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Advisory issued 30 Jul 2026; federal PSA updated 6 Aug 2026

items.title: Cisco ASA and FTD VPN zero-day exploited to reload firewalls, added to CISA KEV
items.content_text: Cisco has patched CVE-2026-20349, a flaw in the remote-access SSL VPN service of Secure Firewall ASA and Secure Firewall Threat Defense software that attackers are exploiting to force appliances offline. A specially crafted HTTP request causes an unexpected reload and a denial-of-service condition, with no authentication and no user interaction required. Cisco’s PSIRT confirmed active exploitation in August, and CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue with a federal remediation deadline of 14 August. Hot fixes cover ASA 9.16, 9.18, 9.20, 9.22, 9.23 and 9.24 and FTD 7.0, 7.2, 7.4, 7.6, 7.7 and 10.0. For a water utility the significance is availability: if this appliance is how your SCADA vendor, integrator or on-call operator reaches the plant, an attacker can remove that path at will — and the current PLC campaign is precisely the situation in which you would want remote visibility to work.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Cisco security advisory and CISA KEV catalogue — reported by Help Net Security and SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Exploitation confirmed and KEV listed Aug 2026; reported 13 Aug 2026

items.title: August ICS Patch Tuesday: maximum-severity missing authentication in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced
items.content_text: Siemens published ten advisories in the August cycle. The most serious, SSA-834709, covers a maximum-severity missing authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices allowing a remote, unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the underlying server with elevated privileges. Siemens also fixed a critical code execution flaw in Siveillance Video Management Servers, high-severity issues across Solid Edge, Simcenter Nastran, Siemens License Server, Simcenter Femap, Parasolid and Logo! Soft Comfort, and medium-severity issues in Ruggedcom devices and Desigo controllers. Schneider Electric published advisories for NetBotz 5 and PowerChute Serial Shutdown, and Phoenix Contact issued one covering multiple PLCnext firmware flaws exploitable for denial of service, unexpected behaviour or malicious SQL queries. For water utilities the IoT2050 and PLCnext items are the ones most likely to be sitting in a data-collection or edge role at a remote site rather than in a plant control cabinet.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Siemens ProductCERT SSA-834709, Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact advisories — summarised by SecurityWeek

items.title: Four more exploited flaws added to KEV on 18 August, including Windows IKE and VMware vCenter
items.content_text: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 August: CVE-2026-33824 in Microsoft Internet Key Exchange, CVE-2026-55040 in Microsoft SharePoint, CVE-2026-59310 in Broadcom VMware vCenter and CVE-2026-65400 in Apple macOS. Two further additions followed on 20 August, both in TrueConf Server. For water utilities the IKE and vCenter entries carry the most weight. IKE is the service that terminates site-to-site tunnels to remote pump stations, towers and lift stations, and to vendor networks — the same links you are being told to use instead of exposing devices directly. vCenter is often the management plane for the virtual infrastructure hosting historians, HMI servers and engineering workstations, where a compromise is a hypervisor problem rather than an application one. Neither is an ICS product, which is exactly why they tend to sit outside the OT patch cycle and inside someone else’s.

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Added 18 Aug 2026; two further additions 20 Aug 2026

items.title: CISA publishes an advisory for flaws in Malcolm, its own free OT monitoring suite
items.content_text: Advisory ICSA-26-230-01 covers vulnerabilities in Malcolm, the network traffic analysis suite CISA distributes free for OT and ICS environments. The flaws could allow an attacker to cause a denial-of-service condition or execute arbitrary code, and affect Malcolm versions below 26.06.1, below 26.07.0 and up to and including 26.07.1. The same day CISA published ICSA-26-230-02, covering a stack overflow in Siemens Simcenter Nastran that can lead to remote code execution if a user is tricked into running the affected binary with a malicious string; Siemens has released fixed versions. Malcolm matters more to this sector than its install base suggests: it is the tool many small and mid-size water utilities deploy precisely because they have no budget for commercial OT monitoring, it is usually placed on a span or tap with visibility into the entire control network, and it is rarely on anyone’s patch inventory.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-230-01 and ICSA-26-230-02

items.title: Johnson Controls Airwall arbitrary file read, plus Hitachi Energy and ANDRITZ in the mid-August batch
items.content_text: CISA’s advisories in the 11 to 13 August window included Johnson Controls Airwall, ICSA-26-225-03, with an arbitrary file read vulnerability; Johnson Controls recommends applying version 4.1.0 or later to all Airwall deployments. The same batch covered Hitachi Energy APM Edge, ICSA-26-225-04, where CVE-2026-43284 and CVE-2026-43500 let a local unprivileged user escalate to root in versions up to and including 6.10, and ANDRITZ HIPASE-250 and 250 SCALA. Airwall is the one most likely to appear in a water utility: it is frequently deployed as the overlay providing secure remote connectivity to remote sites and vendor support, which is the same architecture federal guidance is currently urging utilities to adopt in place of direct device exposure. A file-read flaw in the product mediating that access is worth treating as more than a routine advisory.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-225-03 and ICSA-26-225-04 — roundup via WaterISAC

items.title: Industry groups press Congress for a water reliability organisation modelled on NERC
items.content_text: In the wake of the attacks, federal authorities and industry groups are pushing together for greater oversight and more resources. The National Association of Water Companies is urging Congress to pass bipartisan legislation creating a water risk and resilience organisation that would advise the EPA on developing uniform cybersecurity standards, operating along the lines of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation. Its chief executive told Cybersecurity Dive that no one should be exempt from meeting compliance standards. The American Water Works Association has written to House and Senate leaders seeking additional funding, wider eligibility for cybersecurity training and improved information sharing. The EPA held a call with hundreds of water industry stakeholders in late July. None of this creates an obligation today, but a sector historically resistant to mandatory cyber standards asking for them is a meaningful shift in posture.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: National Association of Water Companies and AWWA statements — reported by Cybersecurity Dive

items.title: New York awards nine million dollars to strengthen cybersecurity at 153 water systems
items.content_text: New York has announced roughly nine million dollars in grants to help local governments assess and improve cyber defences at 153 water systems, alongside the state’s cybersecurity regulations for water utilities. The grants are structured in two tiers: Tier 1 covers assessment work such as penetration testing and risk assessments, and Tier 2 covers implementation including firewalls, network segmentation and incident response planning. A source familiar with the programme said New York was not among the states affected by the recent attacks. The relevance beyond New York is the structure rather than the sum. Assessment-only funding tends to produce reports that sit unimplemented; separating an implementation tier acknowledges that the binding constraint at small utilities is usually the capital to act on findings, not the findings themselves. Operators in other states can reasonably point to this design when arguing for state or revolving-fund support.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Office of the Governor of New York — reported by SecurityWeek
